notes:
I found sources for most verses. Some gaps are listed at the end.

**Acts 10:25–48: Research notes**

**v. 25 (Cornelius bows down to Peter)**
- Guzik: Cornelius probably took Peter for a special man of God. This reaction was understandable, though wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- Precept Austin suggests Cornelius didn't fully understand that only Christ may be worshipped, and that as a Roman he would have been taught emperor worship. It also cites the NET Bible note: the act showed piety and respect, but it was an act based on ignorance, as Peter's remark in v. 26 indicates. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary

**v. 26 ("Stand up… I am only a man")**
- John Stott (quoted on Precept Austin): Peter refused both to be treated as a god by Cornelius and to treat Cornelius as unclean. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Guzik: Cornelius and Peter honoured each other, as Romans 12:10 teaches. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- **Where traditions differ (worship of saints):** Calvin (Reformed) thinks Cornelius didn't mistake Peter for God but went too far in his reverence. Calvin argues that if the Catholic distinction of *dulia* (lesser honour) were valid, Peter should have told Cornelius to stop at *dulia*. Instead Peter gave only one reason: he is a man. https://www.ccel.org/study/Acts_10
- Guzik makes a similar point against the custom of kissing the toe of Peter's statue in St Peter's, Rome, calling it undue reverence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- I didn't find a Catholic reply on this verse.

**v. 27 (Peter goes inside)**
- Guzik (quoted on Precept Austin): this short verse matters a great deal. Jewish custom strictly forbade entering a Gentile's home, so by going in Peter showed he had learned the lesson of the sheet vision. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Peter found that many people were expecting him, which encouraged him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_010.cfm

**v. 28 ("unlawful… to associate with a foreigner")**
- Stott (quoted on Precept Austin): No orthodox Jew would ever enter the home of a Gentile, even a God-fearer, or invite such into his home. This deep prejudice had to be overcome before Gentiles could join the church as equals. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Word study: the Greek word for "foreigner" (*allophylos*) appears only here in the New Testament. The idea was that a Gentile was ceremonially unclean and would make a Jew unclean too. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-10-commentary
- F. F. Bruce: God's cleansing of food in the vision was a picture of God cleansing people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Stott (quoted by Guzik): the chapter is less about Cornelius's conversion than about Peter's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/

**v. 29 ("I came without objection")**
- A. T. Robertson: the word means "without answering back." Peter's objections had been made in the vision. Now He had stepped over the line of Jewish custom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Biblical Illustrator: Cornelius sent for Peter to hear words by which he would be saved, so salvation and truth go together. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-10.html

**vv. 30–32 (Cornelius's vision)**
- Guzik: the angel was seen in a vision (Acts 10:3). Cornelius's mention of praying at the ninth hour (3 p.m., a usual Jewish prayer time) confirms he was praying when it came. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- Guzik on v. 31: Cornelius was not yet born again, yet God heard his prayers and remembered his giving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- John Phillips: Cornelius's prayers and gifts couldn't save him; only Christ's blood could. They were accepted as evidence that he would respond when given more light. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Jack Arnold: the angel didn't preach the gospel, because God gave that task to people, not angels. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Biblical Illustrator: the angel's words change in the retelling, from what Peter "shall tell thee… to do" (v. 6) to "shall speak unto thee" (v. 32, KJV). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-10.html

**v. 33 ("we are all here in the presence of God")**
- Precept Austin: God was preparing both the hearer (Cornelius) and the messenger (Peter), which shows his sovereign hand in salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Robertson: "you were kind enough to come" was a normal way of saying thanks. Cornelius praised Peter's courage in breaking with Jewish custom and wasn't offended by the implied Jewish superiority. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Biblical Illustrator: Cornelius sent for Peter at once because he was eager to hear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-10.html

**v. 34 ("God does not show favouritism")**
- Guzik: this is the basis for taking the gospel to Gentiles. It went against the common Jewish belief of the time that God favoured Jews over Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- Robertson: Peter only grasped this truth fully once he had crossed Cornelius's threshold. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary

**v. 35 ("welcomes those… who fear Him and do what is right")**
- Traditional reading: "every nation" comes first in the Greek for emphasis. Peter isn't teaching salvation by works, since v. 43 ties forgiveness to believing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Guzik: Peter doesn't mean such people are already right with God. He means their nationality doesn't shut them out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- **Was Cornelius already saved?** Piper (Baptist) says no. Cornelius had to hear the gospel to be saved. "Acceptable" means God treats his search as genuine and works wonders to bring him the gospel. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-god-has-cleansed-do-not-call-common
- Steven Cole: when someone seeks God, God is drawing them. Cornelius crossed into salvation during the sermon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Ellicott (Anglican, writing on v. 4) gives a different emphasis. Cornelius's good works came from God's grace already at work in him. He had the faith of Hebrews 11:6 (believing God exists and rewards those who seek him), though he didn't yet connect it with Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/10.htm
- Biblical Illustrator goes broader: God accepts whoever is right, whether he be a Socrates or a Paul, a Cornelius or a Peter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-10.html
- Catholic view: a Catholic Answers article uses Cornelius as a biblical example of God giving the Holy Spirit outside the sacrament of baptism, in its argument about how non-Christians can be saved. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/salvation-for-non-christians-explained-sola-scriptura

**v. 36 ("Lord of all")**
- Guzik: the phrase shows that Jesus is God, and "all" means Jew and Gentile alike. Peter had one gospel for everyone, not different sermons for different groups. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-10/
- Constable: the Lord of all (v. 36) is also the Judge of all (v. 42). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/10-42.html

**vv. 37–38 (Jesus anointed with the Spirit and power)**
- "Anointed" translates *chrio*, meaning set apart and empowered for a sacred task. The title Christ (Messiah, "Anointed One") comes from the same word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-1-commentary
- Precept Austin points out that the verse implies Jesus did good by the Spirit's power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_316-17
- Biblical Illustrator: Peter was mainly addressing Cornelius and the soldiers present. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-10.html

**vv. 39–41 (the cross, the resurrection, the chosen witnesses)**
- Ellicott: the risen Jesus is recorded eating with the disciples three times (Luke 24:30, 42; John 21:13). That was the decisive test showing he was no phantom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/10.htm

**v. 42 (Judge of the living and the dead)**
- Gill: "the people" means Gentiles as well as Jews, and the verse refers to the commission in Matthew 28:19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/10-42.htm
- Meyer (on the same page) disagrees: the context means only the Jewish people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/10-42.htm
- Ellicott: Peter and Paul both connect the resurrection with Jesus as the coming Judge. https://biblehub.com/acts/10-42.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the statement assumes the dead will be raised, and short statements like this help explain how the creeds were formed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/10-42.htm
- Calvin: "the living" are those still alive at Christ's return, who will be changed in a moment (1 Corinthians 15:51). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/10-42.html

**v. 43 (forgiveness through faith)**
- Robertson: Peter now saw that Gentiles didn't have to become Jews. They only had to believe in Jesus as the prophets foretold. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- GotQuestions (on baptism and salvation) notes that Peter links forgiveness to believing, with no mention of baptism at this point. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-Acts-2-38.html

**v. 44 (the Spirit falls on the listeners)**
- Robertson: here the Spirit came before baptism, unlike Acts 8 and 19. Nobody expected it, and it was clear proof that these Gentiles had been converted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Lowell Johnson calls vv. 44–48 the "Gentile Pentecost." https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson

**v. 45 (the Jewish believers are astonished)**
- Precept Austin: these were the six Jewish believers from Joppa. They hadn't seen the vision and probably shared the common bias against Gentiles. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- Luke uses the same verb, "poured out" (*ekcheo*), here as at Pentecost. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary

**v. 46 (speaking in tongues and praising God): a major point of difference**
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):** Peter knew believers at Cornelius' house had received the Holy Spirit because they spoke in tongues, just like on the Day of Pentecost. https://news.ag.org/en/article-repository/news/2019/06/spirit-baptism-how-do-we-know
- The AG's official position cites this passage both for Spirit baptism as an experience separate from and after the new birth, and for tongues as its first visible sign. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/200501/200501_071_BaptismHS.cfm
- An AG position paper notes that in Acts 10 there's no sign the languages were understood or identified. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Baptism-in-the-Holy-Spirit
- The AG's Enrichment Journal admits the main objection: critics say doctrine shouldn't be built on stories in Acts. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/top/Holy_Spirit/200702.cfm
- **Baptist/evangelical:** Steven Cole says every Christian receives the Spirit at salvation. He sees the tongues in Acts 2, 10 and 19 as unique events that won't be repeated, and says the Bible nowhere expects all believers to speak in tongues. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-1-commentary
- Lowell Johnson: the tongues were a sign for the Jewish believers present, not for the Gentiles, proving the Gentiles stood on equal footing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson
- **Reformed:** Donald Macleod notes that Luke treats this as exactly parallel to Pentecost, yet says simply that they "received" the Spirit. https://www.monergism.com/baptism-spirit

**v. 47 ("Can anyone withhold the water?"): a major point of difference**
- Traditional reading: Peter's point is that Gentiles received salvation in the same way as the Jews at Pentecost, so they stand on equal footing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Peter reasons from the reality to the sign. Those God has marked with his Spirit should receive baptism, and since the Spirit came before baptism, he showeth that the Spirit is not included in baptism. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/acts/10-47.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** they were already members of Christ's spiritual body, yet Peter still required water baptism so they would become members of the Christian Church. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/acts/10-47.html
- **Evangelical/Baptist:** GotQuestions says forgiveness and the Spirit clearly came before baptism, so baptism isn't required for salvation. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-Acts-2-38.html
- The Berean Study Bible notes on BibleHub agree: baptism publicly identified them with Christ and didn't earn salvation. https://biblehub.com/acts/10-47.htm
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers says this is the only recorded case of receiving the Spirit before baptism. The Church teaches God isn't bound by the sacraments (Catechism 1257). Peter baptised anyway, the writer suggests, as a kind of "conditional baptism." https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-baptize-cornelius-if-he-already-received-the-holy-spirit
- Another Catholic Answers article disputes the use of this verse to deny that baptism forgives sins (Acts 2:38). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/in-baptism-our-sins-are-forgiven
- **Augustine:** Cornelius would have been guilty of despising the sacrament if he had refused baptism after receiving the Spirit. Just as Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, Cornelius was sanctified first and received the sacrament of regeneration afterwards. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/14084.htm

**v. 48 (baptised in Jesus' name)**
- Augustine: even though baptism might seem unnecessary after such clear signs of the Spirit, they were baptised, with apostolic authority behind it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/14084.htm
- Kistemaker (quoted on Precept Austin) links the baptism to the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-10-commentary

**Gaps:**
- My tool limit ran out before I got the full verse notes from Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary for vv. 25–41 and 43–48. Ellicott's chapter page cut off at v. 15, and the Precept Austin and Enduring Word pages were also cut short. So I have nothing specific on vv. 39–40 ("hanging on a tree"), and v. 48 is thin.
- I found nothing on this passage from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), bibleodyssey.org or oca.org (Orthodox), and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. The only modern-scholarship items are the NET note on v. 25 and Meyer on v. 42.
